name: Heart (overview)
func: A muscular pump in the middle of the chest with four chambers. The right side pumps blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen; the left side pumps oxygen-rich blood to the whole body, about 100,000 beats a day.

levels.kid:
Your **heart** is a strong muscle about the size of your **fist**, sitting in the middle of your chest and tipped a little to the left.

It is a **pump**. Every time it beats, it squeezes blood out through tubes to every part of your body, carrying **oxygen** and food to all your cells.

Inside, the heart has **four rooms**: two on the top and two on the bottom. The right side sends blood to your **lungs** to pick up fresh air. The left side sends that fresh blood out to your whole body.

Little doors called **valves** open and shut to keep blood going the right way. That "lub-dub" sound you hear is the doors closing!
levels.hs:
The **heart** sits in the **middle mediastinum** of the chest, between the two **lungs**, behind the **sternum**, and resting on the **diaphragm**. About two-thirds of it lies left of the midline, and its pointed tip, the **apex**, sits near the 5th intercostal space on the left. It is wrapped in a double-layered sac, the **pericardium**.

It has four chambers. The two upper **atria** receive blood, and the two lower **ventricles** pump it out. A muscular wall, the **septum**, separates the right and left sides.

Blood follows two loops:
- **Pulmonary circulation**: the **right atrium** receives oxygen-poor blood from the body through the **venae cavae**, the **right ventricle** pumps it through the **pulmonary trunk** to the lungs.
- **Systemic circulation**: oxygen-rich blood returns through the **pulmonary veins** to the **left atrium**, and the thick-walled **left ventricle** pumps it into the **aorta** and out to the body.

Four **valves** keep blood flowing one way: the **tricuspid** and **mitral** valves between atria and ventricles, and the **pulmonary** and **aortic** valves at the exits. Their closing makes the "**lub-dub**" heart sounds.

The heart's own muscle is fed by the **coronary arteries**. A natural pacemaker, the **sinoatrial (SA) node**, starts each beat.
levels.college:
**Orientation**: the heart is rotated so the **right ventricle** forms most of the **anterior surface**, the **left atrium** forms most of the **base** (posterior surface, next to the esophagus), and the **left ventricle** forms the apex and much of the left border. The right border is mostly the right atrium; the inferior (diaphragmatic) surface is mainly the left and right ventricles.

**Wall layers**: **epicardium** (visceral serous pericardium), **myocardium** (cardiac muscle) and **endocardium**. A **fibrous skeleton** of dense connective tissue rings the valves and electrically insulates the atria from the ventricles.

**Conduction system**: the **SA node** (at the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium) → atrial muscle → the **AV node** (in the triangle of Koch) → the **bundle of His** → **right and left bundle branches** → **Purkinje fibers**. The AV node delays the signal so the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract.

**Coronary arteries** arise from the aortic sinuses just above the aortic valve:
- The **left main** divides into the **left anterior descending (LAD)**, supplying the front of the left ventricle and most of the septum, and the **circumflex**.
- The **right coronary artery (RCA)** supplies the right ventricle and, in most people (**right dominance**, about 70–85%), the **posterior descending artery** and the SA and AV nodes.
Most venous blood drains through the **coronary sinus** into the right atrium.

**Cardiac cycle**: in **systole** the ventricles contract (AV valves closed, S1); in **diastole** they relax and fill (semilunar valves closed, S2). Coronary flow to the left ventricle occurs mainly during **diastole**.
levels.phd:
**Excitation–contraction coupling**: an action potential opens **L-type calcium channels** (Cav1.2) in the T-tubules; the small calcium entry triggers a large release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum through **ryanodine receptors (RyR2)**, a process called **calcium-induced calcium release**. Calcium binds **troponin C**, letting myosin bind actin. Relaxation requires **SERCA2a** to pump calcium back, regulated by **phospholamban**, which beta-adrenergic stimulation phosphorylates to speed relaxation.

**Frank–Starling law**: greater filling stretches sarcomeres toward optimal length and increases myofilament calcium sensitivity, so stroke volume rises with venous return. The giant protein **titin** sets passive stiffness and contributes to length-dependent activation.

**Pacemaking** in the SA node combines a **membrane clock** (the funny current, **If**, through **HCN4** channels, plus T-type calcium currents) and a **calcium clock** (spontaneous SR calcium release driving the sodium–calcium exchanger). Sympathetic stimulation speeds both; vagal acetylcholine slows them, partly by opening **GIRK** potassium channels.

**Development**: the heart is the first functioning organ in the embryo, beating by about day 22. It arises from the **first and second heart fields**; the second heart field (marked by **Islet-1**) forms the right ventricle and outflow tract. Key transcription factors include **NKX2-5**, **GATA4**, **TBX5** and **HAND2**; mutations cause congenital heart defects. **Cardiac neural crest** cells septate the outflow tract into aorta and pulmonary trunk.

Adult cardiomyocytes renew very slowly, under about 1% per year (carbon-14 dating, Bergmann and colleagues), which is why infarcted muscle heals by scarring. Zebrafish and neonatal mice can regenerate heart muscle, a major research focus.
levels.expert:
**Exam**: palpate the **apex beat** (normally 5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line); a displaced beat suggests an enlarged heart. Listen at the four classic areas: aortic (right 2nd intercostal space), pulmonary (left 2nd), tricuspid (left lower sternal edge) and mitral (apex). Extra sounds: **S3** (heart failure in adults, normal in many young people) and **S4** (stiff ventricle). Murmurs: **aortic stenosis** (ejection systolic, radiating to the carotids), **mitral regurgitation** (pansystolic, radiating to the axilla).

**Acute coronary syndromes**: plaque rupture and clot block a coronary artery. ST elevation in leads V1–V4 suggests an **LAD** blockage; II, III and aVF an inferior (usually **RCA**) infarct. Diagnosis uses the **ECG** and **high-sensitivity troponin**. Treatment includes antiplatelet and anticoagulant medication and urgent **percutaneous coronary intervention (stenting)**; multivessel disease may need **coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG)**.

**Heart failure** is classified by ejection fraction (reduced, mildly reduced or preserved); **BNP** levels and **echocardiography** guide diagnosis. **Cardiac tamponade** shows **Beck triad** (low blood pressure, raised neck veins, muffled heart sounds) and pulsus paradoxus, treated by drainage.

**Congenital heart disease** affects about 1 in 100 births: ventricular septal defect, tetralogy of Fallot, transposition of the great arteries. **Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy** is a leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes.

**Imaging**: echocardiography, cardiac MRI, CT coronary angiography and catheter angiography. **Neurosurgical link**: atrial fibrillation and other heart conditions are a major source of **embolic stroke**, and a **patent foramen ovale** can let clots cross into the brain.

keyPoints: Sits in the middle mediastinum, apex at the left 5th intercostal space
Four chambers; right side → lungs, left side → body
Four valves: tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral, aortic
Conduction: SA node → AV node → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibers
LAD, circumflex and RCA supply the heart muscle; blockage → heart attack

test.q: Which chamber forms most of the front (anterior) surface of the heart?
test.explain: The heart is rotated so the right ventricle faces forward; the left atrium forms the back (base).

test.q: The heart's natural pacemaker is the:
test.explain: The SA node at the SVC–right atrium junction fires first and sets the rate.

test.q: The valve between the left atrium and left ventricle is the ______ valve.
test.explain: The mitral (bicuspid) valve has two leaflets.

test.q: ST elevation in leads V1–V4 suggests blockage of which artery?
test.explain: The LAD supplies the anterior wall and septum, seen in the precordial leads.

test.q: Low blood pressure, raised neck veins and muffled heart sounds form ______ triad.
test.explain: Beck triad suggests cardiac tamponade, fluid squeezing the heart in the pericardium.
